issues.issue: Defining Third Party negatively as anyone other than an Employee or a person 'acting in collusion with an Employee' leaves 'collusion' undefined, so a deceived employee's participation may or may not defeat third-party status.

Exclusion 12(n) removes loss due to listed frauds 'or other fraudulent, dishonest or criminal act ... committed by any authorized representative of an Insured'; both the catch-all after the enumerated frauds and the undefined 'authorized representative' leave the exclusion's reach uncertain.

Sub-paragraph (b) (loss of trade secrets or confidential information) is deleted and replaced by the Privacy and Data Breach endorsement (c146), so the printed list of exclusions no longer states the operative terms.

'Any agent, broker, factor, commission merchant, consignee, contractor, independent contractor, subcontractor or other similar representative' ends in a catch-all whose reach against the enumerated specifics is uncertain, particularly against the Employee definition that includes leased and temporary staff.

'Kidnap, ransom or other extortion payment (as distinct from Robbery) surrendered to any person as a result of a threat' does not say how a fraudulently induced payment is distinguished from an extorted one.

Exclusion 17 is deleted in its entirety by Endorsement No. 4 to the Crime section, yet the printed exclusion remains in the policy text; the operative position on Insuring Clause 5 losses can only be read from the endorsement.

This exclusion removes from Insuring Clause 8 loss caused by 'any forgery or alteration of, on or in any written instrument' — precisely what the definition of Credit Card Fraud (c082) requires for the coverage to attach, leaving the grant nearly nullified apart from the two provisos.

Exclusion 19 is rewritten 'in its entirety' twice over by endorsements effective the same date — the Conversion endorsement (c149), which drops the 60-day notice requirement and adds a discovery-before-termination test, and the Amend Exclusion 19 endorsement (c156), which keeps it. The printed exclusion cannot be reconciled with both.
Liability is limited to property owned by or held by 'the Organization', while Insuring Clause 1 (c066) pays for loss sustained by 'an Insured', a term that includes ERISA and Non-ERISA Plans.

The ERISA version of Insuring Clause 1 covers 'a fraudulent or dishonest act', a materially wider trigger than the defined Theft or Forgery used in the clause it replaces, and 'dishonest' is left undefined.

This deletes 'sixty (60) days' wherever it appears in Exclusion 19, but the Conversion endorsement's replacement Exclusion 19 (c149) contains no such words at all, while the Amend Exclusion 19 endorsement (c156) reinstates them. The instruction cannot be applied coherently.
The blanket disapplication of any retention for ERISA Plan loss sits against Subsection 25 (c132), which makes liability apply only to loss in excess of the Item 3 Retention.

This first paragraph is replaced 'in its entirety' by the Conversion endorsement (c150), which converts the trigger from coverage 'after the effective date' of acquisition to coverage for loss 'Discovered after' it; the printed text no longer states the operative rule.

'Such information as the Company in its sole discretion may require' and 'any reasonable additional premium required by the Company', with automatic voidance for failure, are one-sided and leave the insured's obligation without an ascertainable limit.

Subsection 24 is deleted in its entirety by paragraph (3) of the Conversion endorsement, which also deletes all references to it; the printed text therefore contradicts the operative policy, and Subsection 25 (c128) still opens 'Subject to Subsection 24'.
This paragraph forms part of Subsection 24, which the Conversion endorsement deletes in its entirety, while Subsection 12 (c047) separately terminates prior Company bonds at inception.
This limitation belongs to Subsection 24, which paragraph (3) of the Conversion endorsement deletes in its entirety, leaving no prior-loss limit to apply.

It is expressly 'Subject to Subsection 24', which the Conversion endorsement deletes, and it is itself replaced by paragraph (4) of that endorsement (c151), which shifts the trigger from loss sustained during the Policy Period to loss Discovered during the Policy Period.
'Any series of related acts, casualties or events' and acts in which the same Third Party is 'concerned or implicated' set the aggregation boundary in language whose limits are not defined.
The single Retention applies to 'each loss', while Insuring Clause 10 (c075) and the ERISA provision (c121) disapply any retention and Item 3 (c064) states one unallocated figure.
Imputing all knowledge to all Insureds sits against the Discovery definition (c084), which confines discovery to an Executive or Insurance Representative and excludes knowledge of a complicit one.
'At the earliest practicable moment' is a vague standard laid alongside the fixed ninety-day and six-month outer limits, leaving unclear when the condition precedent is actually breached.

Making notice an unqualified condition precedent cannot be squared with the New York Late Notice endorsement (c050), which provides that late notice does not invalidate coverage absent prejudice, or with Subsection 5 of the General Terms (c033).
The lettered sub-paragraphs (a) and (b) are printed detached from the text that follows them, so which limitation period attaches to which claim is not clear from the provision as written.
Valuation is fixed by reference to the day of Discovery, whereas Subsection 6 of the General Terms (c034) fixes foreign-currency conversion at the date loss is due or judgment becomes final.

Saying the coverage section is 'null and void' to the extent of other collectible insurance, then providing that it 'shall cover such loss' in excess of that insurance, states the same rule in two inconsistent registers.
It overlaps Exclusion 12(m) (c108), which addresses the same excess-of-other-recovery position for property in the custody of banks and carriers by a different mechanism.
It replaces subparagraph (a) of the Executive definition, but the unamended text (c087) remains printed in the coverage section, so the operative list of Executives appears twice in different forms.

'Any similar type of nonpublic information' follows a list running from patents to health information, and 'loss involving the disclosure ... or use of' confidential information has no stated boundary; how far the catch-all reaches beyond the enumerated categories is genuinely open.

The carve-back preserves only loss 'otherwise covered under Insuring Clause 6, Funds Transfer Fraud Coverage', leaving the Computer Fraud grant in Insuring Clause 5 (c070) exposed to an exclusion broad enough to swallow it.

This replacement Exclusion 19 requires loss to be sustained and Discovered before termination, with no post-termination notice window, while the Amend Exclusion 19 endorsement (c156), effective the same date, rewrites the same exclusion 'in its entirety' with a 60-day post-termination discovery and notice regime. Both cannot govern.

It rewrites the first paragraph of Subsection 23 so that new subsidiaries are covered only for loss 'Discovered after' the acquisition, displacing the printed text (c123) which grants coverage after the effective date of the acquisition.

It converts the trigger to loss Discovered during the Policy Period, contradicting the printed Subsection 25 (c128), which limits liability to loss sustained during the Policy Period, and sitting against the Amended Exclusion 19 (c156), which allows discovery within sixty days after termination.

'All other terms ... remain unchanged' has to operate alongside a further endorsement (c156) that changes one of the very provisions this endorsement rewrote, so which endorsement survives is left to construction.

This rewrites Exclusion 19 'in its entirety' to require Discovery and written notice within sixty days after termination, while the Conversion endorsement (c149), effective the same date, rewrites the same exclusion in its entirety to require discovery before termination with no notice window. The policy contains two irreconcilable versions of Exclusion 19.
'All other terms ... remain unchanged' does not resolve its relationship with the Conversion endorsement (c149), which had already replaced the same Exclusion 19 in different terms.
